questions.subject: network-theory
questions.ref: Network Theorems For DC & Miscellaneous Topics Q1
questions.question: A dc circuit shown in figure has a voltage source \(V\), a current source \(I\) and several resistors. A particular resistor \(R\) dissipates a power of \(4\text{ Watts}\) when \(V\) alone is active. The same resistor \(R\) dissipates a power of \(9\text{ Watts}\) when \(I\) alone is active. The power dissipated by \(R\) when both sources are active will be
questions.explanation:
Method Superposition Theorem
(i) Let the voltage source \(V\) alone be active.
Replace the current source by its internal resistance, i.e., an open circuit. The current through resistor \(R\) is \(I_1\). Power dissipated in \(R\) is \[P_1=I_1^2R=4~\text{W}\] (ii) Let the current source \(I\) alone be active.
Replace the voltage source by its internal resistance, i.e., a short circuit. The current through resistor \(R\) is \(I_2\). Power dissipated in \(R\) is \[P_2=I_2^2R=9~\text{W}\] (iii) When both sources are active
According to the Superposition Theorem, \[I=I_1\pm I_2\] Therefore, \[P = (I_1\pm I_2)^2R = I_1^2R+I_2^2R\pm2I_1I_2R\] where, \[I_1I_2R = \sqrt{I_1^2R\times I_2^2R} = \sqrt{P_1P_2} = \sqrt{4\times9} = 6~\text{W}\] \[\Rightarrow P = 4+9\pm2(6)\] Thus, \[P_{\max}=25~\text{W}, \qquad P_{\min}=1~\text{W}\]
Method Direct Formula
The maximum and minimum power are given by \[P_{\max} = \left(\sqrt{P_1}+\sqrt{P_2}\right)^2\] \[P_{\max} = (\sqrt{4}+\sqrt{9})^2 = (2+3)^2 = 25~\text{W}\] Similarly, \[P_{\min} = \left(\sqrt{P_1}-\sqrt{P_2}\right)^2\] \[P_{\min} = (\sqrt{4}-\sqrt{9})^2 = (2-3)^2 = 1~\text{W}\] Hence, the correct answers are \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }1~\text{W}} \quad \text{and} \quad \boxed{\textbf{D. }25~\text{W}}\]

questions.question: The value of the resistance, \(R\) connected across the terminals, \(A\) and \(B\) (ref. figure), which will absorb the maximum power, is
questions.explanation: Using the Maximum Power Transfer Theorem, \(R=R_{TH}\) Deactivate the independent voltage source by replacing it with a short circuit. The modified circuit is shown below. The short circuit makes nodes \(C\) and \(D\) equipotential. Hence, \[R_{TH} = (3\parallel6) + (4\parallel4)\] Now, \[3\parallel6 = \frac{3\times6}{3+6} = 2~\text{k}\Omega, \ \qquad \ 4\parallel4 = \frac{4\times4}{4+4} = 2~\text{k}\Omega\] Therefore, \[R_{TH} = 2+2 = 4~\text{k}\Omega\] Hence, \[R=R_{TH}=4~\text{k}\Omega\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }4.00~\text{k}\Omega}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: The current i(t), through a \(10\Omega\) resistor in series with an inductance is given by \[i(t) = 3+4\sin{(100t+45^{\circ})}+4\sin{(300t+60^{\circ})}A\] The RMS value of the current and the power dissipated in the circuit are :
questions.explanation: The RMS value of current i(t) is given by \[I_{RMS}=\sqrt{I_o^2+I_1^2/2+I_3^2/2}\] Substituting, \[I_{RMS}=\sqrt{3^2+4^2/2+4^2/2}=5A\] Power dissipated in a network is given by \[P_{diss}=I_{RMS}^2R=5^2\times10=250W\] \[\boxed{(c) 5A, 250 W\,\text{respectively}}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: A series R-L-C circuit has a Q of 100 and an impedance of (100+j0)\(\Omega\) at its resonant angular frequency of \(10^7\) rad/sec. The values of R and L are : R = ohms and L = ohms.
questions.explanation: At resonant frequency, the imaginary part of impedance becomes 0, and the impedance equals the resistance present in the circuit. \[R = 100\Omega \,\text{from given information that circuit has an impedance of (100+j0)$\Omega$ at its resonant angular frequency}\] We know that for a series RLC circuit, quality factor is given by \[Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R}\] Here, \(\omega_0=10^7 rad/s\) , Q = 100 and \(R = 100\Omega\) Therefore, \(L=\frac{QR}{\omega_0}=\frac{100\times100}{10^7}=0.001 H\) \[\boxed{R=100\Omega, L=0.001H}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: Two 2H inductance coils are connected in series and are also magnetically coupled to each other the coefficient of coupling being 0.1. The total inductance of the combination can be
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
The two inductors in series can be either additively or subtractively coupled. We know that mutual inductance and coefficient of coupling are related as \[M=k\sqrt{L_1L_2}=0.1\sqrt{2\times2}=0.2H\] Additive coupling :
\[L_{eq}=L_1+L_2+2M=2+2+2\times0.2=4.4H\] Subtractive coupling :
\[L_{eq}=L_1+L_2-2M=2+2-2\times0.2=3.6H\] \[\boxed{4.4H, 3.6H}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The RMS value of a rectangular wave of period \(T\), having a value of \(+V\) for a duration, \(T_1 (<T)\) and \(-V\) for the duration, \(T - T_1 = T_2\), equals
questions.explanation:
The RMS (Root Mean Square) value of a periodic signal \(v(t)\) with period \(T\) is calculated using the formula: \[V_{rms} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} v^2(t) \, dt }\] Based on the problem description, the waveform over one complete period \(T\) is defined as: \(v(t) = +V\) for a duration of \(T_1\) \(v(t) = -V\) for a duration of \(T_2\) where \(T_1 + T_2 = T\). We evaluate the integral by splitting it into the two defined durations: \[V_{rms} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{T} \left( \int_{0}^{T_1} (+V)^2 \, dt + \int_{T_1}^{T} (-V)^2 \, dt \right) }\] Squaring the amplitudes: \[V_{rms} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{T} \left( \int_{0}^{T_1} V^2 \, dt + \int_{T_1}^{T} V^2 \, dt \right) }\] Evaluating the definite integrals: \[V_{rms} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{T} \left( V^2 [t]_{0}^{T_1} + V^2 [t]_{T_1}^{T} \right) }\] \[V_{rms} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{T} \left( V^2 (T_1 - 0) + V^2 (T - T_1) \right) }\] Substitute \(T - T_1 = T_2\): \[V_{rms} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{T} \left( V^2 T_1 + V^2 T_2 \right) }\] \[V_{rms} = \sqrt{ \frac{V^2}{T} (T_1 + T_2) }\] Since the total period \(T = T_1 + T_2\), we substitute \(T\) back into the equation: \[V_{rms} = \sqrt{ \frac{V^2}{T} (T) }\] \[V_{rms} = \sqrt{V^2} = V\] \[\boxed{\text{(A) V}}\]
Key points
  • The RMS value measures the equivalent heating power of a signal, calculated as the square root of the mean of the squared signal over one period.
  • If the absolute magnitude of a signal is constant (e.g., it only switches between \(+V\) and \(-V\)), its squared waveform is a constant flat DC line at \(V^2\). Consequently, its RMS value is simply the magnitude \(V\), regardless of the widths \(T_1\) and \(T_2\).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: Let \(h(t)\) be the impulse response of a linear time invariant system. Then the response of the system for any input \(u(t)\) is
questions.explanation:
Note that here \(u(t)\) is not a unit step function. It is any arbitrary input. For LTI system: \[y(t) = u(t) * h(t)\] By definition of the convolution integral: \[y(t) = \int_{\tau=-\infty}^{\infty} h(\tau)u(t - \tau)d\tau\] or, using the commutative property: \[= \int_{\tau=-\infty}^{\infty} h(t - \tau)u(\tau)d\tau\] If the system is causal, the impulse response must satisfy \(h(t) = 0\) for \(t < 0\). This means \(h(\tau) = 0\) for \(\tau < 0\). Therefore, the lower limit of the integral becomes \(0\): \[= \int_{\tau=0}^{\infty} h(\tau)u(t - \tau)d\tau\] If, in addition to the system being causal, the input \(u(t)\) is also causal, then \(u(t) = 0\) for \(t < 0\). In the integral \(u(t - \tau)\), this means \(u(t - \tau) = 0\) when \(t - \tau < 0\), which implies \(\tau > t\). Therefore, the upper limit of the integral is bounded by \(t\): \[y(t) = \int_{\tau=0}^{t} h(\tau)u(t - \tau)d\tau\]
Key points
  • Convolution Integral: The fundamental relationship for continuous-time LTI systems is \(y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(\tau)x(t-\tau)d\tau\).
  • Causal System limit: A causal system restricts the lower limit to \(0\) because the system cannot respond before the impulse occurs (\(h(t) = 0\) for \(t<0\)).
  • Causal Input limit: A causal input restricts the upper limit to \(t\) because future values of the input (\(x(t-\tau)\) for \(\tau > t\)) are zero.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Notation confusion: Always clarify the meaning of symbols like \(u(t)\) in a specific context. Usually, \(u(t)\) is the unit step, but here it represents an arbitrary input signal (often denoted as \(x(t)\)).
  • Incorrect Limits: Do not automatically use limits from \(0\) to \(t\) unless you are certain both the system and the input signal are causal.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: A \(1.0\,\text{kHz}\) signal is flat - top sampled at the rate of \(1800\,\text{samples/sec}\) and the samples are applied to an ideal rectangular LPF with cut - off frequency of \(1100\,\text{Hz}\), then the output of the filter contains
questions.explanation:
Given the parameters: Message signal frequency, \(f_m = 1.0\,\text{kHz} = 1000\,\text{Hz}\) Sampling rate, \(f_s = 1800\,\text{samples/sec} = 1800\,\text{Hz}\) Cut-off frequency of the ideal LPF, \(f_c = 1100\,\text{Hz}\) When a continuous-time signal is sampled, the spectrum of the sampled signal consists of shifted versions of the original spectrum centered at integer multiples of the sampling frequency. The frequency components present in the sampled signal are given by: \[f_{out} = |n f_s \pm f_m|\] where \(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) Calculating the frequency components for different values of \(n\): For \(n = 0\) (Baseband): \[f_{out} = 1000\,\text{Hz}\] For \(n = 1\) (First harmonic): \[f_{out} = |1800 \pm 1000| \implies 800\,\text{Hz} \text{ and } 2800\,\text{Hz}\] For \(n = 2\) (Second harmonic): \[f_{out} = |3600 \pm 1000| \implies 2600\,\text{Hz} \text{ and } 4600\,\text{Hz}\] The resulting frequency components are \(800\,\text{Hz}\), \(1000\,\text{Hz}\), \(2600\,\text{Hz}\), \(2800\,\text{Hz}\), and so on. The sampled signal is then passed through an ideal rectangular low-pass filter (LPF) with a cut-off frequency of \(1100\,\text{Hz}\). The LPF will only allow frequency components less than \(f_c\) to pass through. Comparing the generated components with the cut-off frequency: \(800\,\text{Hz} < 1100\,\text{Hz}\) (Passed) \(1000\,\text{Hz} < 1100\,\text{Hz}\) (Passed) \(2600\,\text{Hz} > 1100\,\text{Hz}\) (Rejected) Therefore, the output of the filter contains only the \(800\,\text{Hz}\) and \(1000\,\text{Hz}\) components. Note that while flat-top sampling introduces an aperture effect (amplitude distortion shaped by a sinc function), it does not change the location of the frequency components compared to ideal instantaneous sampling. \[\boxed{\text{C) $800\,\text{Hz}$ and $1000\,\text{Hz}$ components. }}\]
Key points
  • The spectrum of a sampled signal contains frequencies at \(n f_s \pm f_m\), where \(n\) is an integer.
  • Aliasing Effect: The Nyquist rate for this signal is \(2f_m = 2000\,\text{Hz}\). Since \(f_s = 1800\,\text{Hz}\) (\(f_s < 2f_m\)), the signal is under-sampled. This causes the lower sideband of the first harmonic (\(1800 - 1000 = 800\,\text{Hz}\)) to fold back into the baseband range, appearing below the original message frequency.
  • An ideal LPF passes all frequencies below its cut-off \(f_c\) with zero attenuation and completely rejects all frequencies above \(f_c\).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The final value theorem is used to find the
options: steady state value of the system output
initial value of the system output
transient behavior of the system output
questions.explanation:
The Final Value Theorem relates the time-domain behavior of a function \(f(t)\) as \(t \to \infty\) to its Laplace transform \(F(s)\) as \(s \to 0\). Mathematically, it is stated as: \[\lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) = \lim_{s \to 0} sF(s)\] Since \(t \to \infty\) corresponds to the condition where all transient responses have died out, evaluating this limit provides the steady-state value of the system output. This allows us to find the steady-state value directly from the \(s\)-domain without needing to compute the full inverse Laplace transform. \[\boxed{\text{A) steady state value of the system output}}\]
Key points
  • Final Value Theorem: Evaluates the steady-state value (\(t \to \infty\)). Formula: \(\lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) = \lim_{s \to 0} sF(s)\).
  • Initial Value Theorem: Evaluates the initial value (\(t \to 0\)). Formula: \(\lim_{t \to 0} f(t) = \lim_{s \to \infty} sF(s)\).
  • The Final Value Theorem is strictly valid only if all the poles of \(sF(s)\) lie in the left half of the \(s\)-plane (i.e., the system is stable).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: If \(\text{L}[f(t)] = \frac{2(s+1)}{s^2+2s+5}\), then \(f(0+)\) and \(f(\infty)\) are given by
questions.explanation:
Given the Laplace transform: \[F(s) = \frac{2(s+1)}{s^2+2s+5}\] Step 1: Find the Initial Value \(f(0+)\) Using the Initial Value Theorem: \[f(0+) = \lim_{s \to \infty} sF(s)\] \[f(0+) = \lim_{s \to \infty} s \left[ \frac{2(s+1)}{s^2+2s+5} \right] = \lim_{s \to \infty} \frac{2s^2+2s}{s^2+2s+5}\] Dividing the numerator and denominator by \(s^2\): \[f(0+) = \lim_{s \to \infty} \frac{2 + \frac{2}{s}}{1 + \frac{2}{s} + \frac{5}{s^2}} = \frac{2 + 0}{1 + 0 + 0} = 2\] Step 2: Find the Final Value \(f(\infty)\) First, we must check if the Final Value Theorem is applicable. We do this by finding the poles of \(sF(s)\). The characteristic equation for the poles is: \[s^2 + 2s + 5 = 0\] The roots are \(s = -1 \pm j2\). Since the real part of all poles is strictly negative (\(-1\)), they lie in the left half of the \(s\)-plane, meaning the system is stable and FVT is applicable. Using the Final Value Theorem: \[f(\infty) = \lim_{s \to 0} sF(s)\] \[f(\infty) = \lim_{s \to 0} s \left[ \frac{2(s+1)}{s^2+2s+5} \right]\] Substituting \(s = 0\): \[f(\infty) = 0 \cdot \left[ \frac{2(0+1)}{0^2+0+5} \right] = 0\] \[\boxed{\text{B) 2, 0 respectively }}\]
Key points
  • Initial Value Theorem (IVT): \(\lim_{t \to 0+} f(t) = \lim_{s \to \infty} sF(s)\).
  • Final Value Theorem (FVT): \(\lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) = \lim_{s \to 0} sF(s)\).
  • Crucial Condition for FVT: The theorem yields a valid result only if all the poles of \(sF(s)\) lie strictly in the left half of the \(s\)-plane.

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: A small concentration of minority carriers is injected into a homogeneous semiconductor crystal at one point. An electric field of \(10\,\text{V/cm}\) is applied across the crystal and this moves the minority carries a distance of \(1\,\text{cm}\) in \(20\,\mu\text{sec}\). The mobility (in \(\text{cm}^2/\text{V-sec}\)) will be
questions.explanation:
The velocity of a charge carrier is defined as the distance traveled per unit time. Based on the given parameters: \[\text{Velocity} = \frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Time}}\] Substituting the values from the problem: \[v_{d} = \frac{1}{20 \times 10^{-6}} = 50,000\,\text{cm/sec}\] The relationship between drift velocity (\(v_{d}\)), mobility (\(\mu\)), and electric field (\(E\)) is given by: \[v_{d} = \mu E\] Rearranging the formula to solve for mobility: \[\mu = \frac{v_{d}}{E} = \frac{50,000}{10} = 5,000\,\text{cm}^2/\text{V-sec}\] \[\boxed{(C) \, 5000}\]
Key points
  • Drift velocity (\(v_{d}\)) is the average velocity attained by charged particles in a material due to an electric field.
  • Mobility (\(\mu\)) characterizes how quickly a charge carrier can move through a metal or semiconductor when pulled by an electric field.

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: In a \(p\)-type Si simple the hole concentration is \(2.25 \times 10^{15}/\text{cm}^3\). The intrinsic carrier concentration is \(1.5 \times 10^{10}/\text{cm}^3\) the electron concentration is
questions.explanation: Given the carrier concentrations in the semiconductor: \[p = 2.25 \times 10^{15}/\text{cm}^3\] \[n_{i} = 1.5 \times 10^{10}/\text{cm}^3\] According to the Mass Action Law: \[n = \frac{n_{i}^2}{p}\] Substituting the given values into the equation: \[n = \frac{(1.5 \times 10^{10})^2}{2.25 \times 10^{15}} = \frac{2.25 \times 10^{20}}{2.25 \times 10^{15}} = 10^5/\text{cm}^3\] \[\boxed{(C) \, 10^5 \text{/cm}^3}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: The probability that an electron in a metal occupies the Fermi level, at any temperature \((T > 0\,\text{K})\)
questions.explanation: At temperatures above \(0\text{ K}\), the Fermi level is defined as the energy level that has a \(50\%\) probability of being occupied by an electron. \[\boxed{(C) \, 0.5}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: The drift velocity of electrons, in silicon
options: is proportional to the electric field for all values of electric field.
is independent of the electric field.
increases at low values of electric field and decreases at high values of electric field exhibiting negative differential resistance.
increases linearly with electric field at low values of electric field and gradually saturates at higher values of electric field.
questions.explanation:
The relationship between drift velocity \(v_{d}\) and the applied electric field \(E\) is governed by carrier mobility \(\mu\): \[v_{d} = \mu E\] The dependence of mobility on the electric field is illustrated in the figure below: [figure unavailable] Based on the variation of \(\mu\) with \(E\):
  1. Low Electric Field (\(E < 10^{3}\,\text{V/m}\)): The mobility of the charge carrier remains almost constant. Consequently, the drift velocity (\(v_{d}\)) increases linearly with the electric field (\(\mu \propto \text{constant} \implies v_{d} \propto E\)).
  2. High Electric Field (\(E > 10^{4}\,\text{V/m}\)): For large applied electric fields, the mobility decreases significantly. Specifically, when \(\mu \propto 1/E\), the drift velocity gradually saturates to a constant value (\(v_{sat}\)), meaning it becomes independent of further increases in the electric field.
\[\boxed{(D)}\] increases linearly with electric field at low values of electric field and gradually saturates at higher values of electric field
Key points
  • At low fields, scattering is dominated by lattice vibrations (phonons) and impurities, keeping \(\mu\) constant.
  • At very high fields, carriers reach a scattering-limited velocity known as saturation velocity (\(v_{sat}\)).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume \(v_{d}\) increases infinitely with \(E\); physical limitations lead to velocity saturation.

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: The depletion capacitance, \(C_J\) of an abruptly \(p\text{-}n\) junction with constant doping on either side varies with R.B. \(V_R\) as,
questions.explanation: The depletion layer capacitance (also known as transition capacitance, \(C_{T}\) or \(C_{j}\)) of a p-n junction diode under reverse bias varies according to the voltage profile across the junction. The general relationship between the depletion capacitance and the reverse bias voltage \(V_{R}\) is expressed as: \[C_{T} \propto V_{R}^{-n}\] Where \(n\) represents the junction grading coefficient. The value of \(n\) depends directly on the nature of the semiconductor doping profile. For a step-graded or abrupt p-n junction, the grading factor is: \[n = \frac{1}{2}\] Substituting \(n = \frac{1}{2}\) for the abrupt junction case given in the problem: \[C_{T} \propto V_{R}^{-1/2}\] Thus, the grading coefficient value corresponds to option C. \[\boxed{(C) \, C_J \propto V_{R}^{-1/2}}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: A Zener diode works on the principle of
options: tunneling of charge carriers across the junction.
diffusion of charge carriers across the junction.
hopping of charge carriers across the junction.
questions.explanation: A Zener diode exhibits a breakdown mechanism that depends directly on the doping concentration of the p-n junction. When both the p-side and n-side are heavily doped, the depletion region becomes extremely narrow. Under a high reverse-bias voltage, a strong electric field is established across this narrow gap. This intense field is sufficient to force valence electrons to breach their covalent bonds and cross the barrier. This physical phenomenon is defined as the tunneling of charge carriers across the junction, which leads the junction directly into zener breakdown. Therefore, the correct option is A. \[\boxed{(A) \text{ tunneling of charge carriers across the junction.}}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: The diffusion potential across a \(p\text{-}n\) junction
options: does not depend on doping concentrations.
increases with increase in doping concentration.
questions.explanation: The built-in diffusion potential, \(V_{bi}\) across an unbiased p-n junction forms due to the diffusion of majority carriers across the metallurgical interface, and is given by: \[V_{bi} = \frac{kT}{q} \ln\left(\frac{N_{A}N_{D}}{n_{i}^2}\right)\] At a constant operating temperature, the thermal voltage term \(V_{T} = \frac{kT}{q}\) and the intrinsic carrier concentration \(n_{i}\) remain fixed. Under these conditions, the contact potential relationship varies logarithmically with respect to the product of the doping concentrations: \[V_{bi} \propto \ln\left(N_{A}N_{D}\right)\] Therefore, an increase in either the acceptor doping concentration (\(N_{A}\)) or the donor doping concentration (\(N_{D}\)) results in a corresponding increase in the contact potential across the junction. Also, intrinsic concentration \(n_i\) depends on bandgap \(E_g\) as \[n_i \propto e^{-\frac{E_g}{kT}}\] At constant temperature, with decrease in bandgap, \(n_i\) increases. This causes a decrease in diffusion potential since the relation can be observed as: \[V_{bi} \propto ln \left( \frac{1}{n_i^2}\right)\] Thus, the only true statement is option D. \[\boxed{(D) \text{ increases with increase in doping concentration}}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: A BJT is said to be operating in the saturation region if
options: both the junctions are reverse biased.
base-emitter junction is reverse biased and base-collector junction is forward biased.
base-emitter junction is forward biased and base-collector junction is reverse biased.
both the junctions are forward biased.
questions.explanation: Both the junctions are forward biased. When emitter base (E-B) junction and collector base (C-B) junction both are forward biased then the BJT is said to be operating in saturation region. \[\boxed{(D)\,\text{both the junctions are forward biased.}}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: The breakdown voltage of a transistor with its base open is \(BV_{CEO}\) and that with emitter open is \(BV_{CBO}\), then
questions.explanation: The relationship between open base breakdown voltage (\(BV_{CEO}\)) of BJT with open emitter voltage (\(BV_{CBO}\)) is given by \[BV_{CEO}=BV_{CBO}\sqrt{\frac{1}{\beta}}\] Since \(\beta>1\), thus \(BV_{CEO}<BV_{CBO}\). \[\boxed{(C)\,BV_{CEO}<BV_{CBO}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: An OP-AMP is used as a zero-crossing detector. If the maximum output available from the OP-AMP is \(\pm 12\text{ V } p-p\), and the slew rate of the OP-AMP is \(12\text{ V}/\mu\text{sec}\), then the maximum frequency(in KHz) of the input signal that can be applied without causing a reduction in the \(p-p\) output is _________.
questions.explanation:
Given:\(V_{pp}=12\,\text{V}\) and \(\text{Slew Rate (SR)}=12\,\text{V}/\mu\text{s}\) For a zero-crossing detector, the output is a square wave switching between the positive and negative saturation levels. During each transition, the output must swing from \(-12\,\text{V}\) to \(+12\,\text{V}\) (or vice versa), i.e., a total voltage change of \[\Delta V=24\,\text{V}\] The minimum time required for one transition is \[t_r=\frac{\Delta V}{SR}\] \[t_r=\frac{24}{12\,\text{V}/\mu\text{s}}\] \[t_r=2\,\mu\text{s}\] There are two such transitions in one complete cycle of the output waveform. Hence, the minimum period of oscillation is \[T_{\min}=2t_r\] \[T_{\min}=4\,\mu\text{s}\] Therefore, the maximum frequency without slew-rate limitation is \[f_{\max}=\frac{1}{T_{\min}}\] \[f_{\max}=\frac{1}{4\times10^{-6}}\] \[f_{\max}=0.25\times10^{6}\,\text{Hz}\] Thus, \[\boxed{f_{\max}=250\,\text{kHz}}\]
Key points
  • Transition time is given by \[t_r=\frac{\Delta V}{SR}.\]
  • Two transitions occur during each cycle of the output waveform.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the given circuit the given figure, if the voltage inputs \(V-\) and \(V+\) are to be amplified by the same amplification factor, the value of R(in kilo ohms) should be
questions.explanation: Given circuit is, Since the op-amp is ideal and has negative feedback, \(V_p = V_n\). Using voltage division at the non-inverting terminal, \[V_{p}=\frac{R}{R+15\,\text{k}\Omega}\,V_{+}\] Applying KCL at the inverting terminal, \[\frac{V_{n}-V_{-}}{10\,\text{k}\Omega}+\frac{V_{n}-V_{o}}{22\,\text{k}\Omega}=0\] Substituting \(V_{n}=V_{p}\), \[\frac{V_{p}-V_{-}}{10\,\text{k}\Omega}+\frac{V_{p}-V_{0}}{22\,\text{k}\Omega}=0\] \[\therefore V_{o}=\left(1+\frac{22}{10}\right)V_{p}-\frac{22}{10}V_{-}\] \[V_{o}=3.2\,V_{p}-2.2\,V_{-}\] \[V_{o}=3.2\left(\frac{R}{R+15\,\text{k}\Omega}\right)V_{+}-2.2V_{-}\] The gains of \(V_{+}\) and \(V_{-}\) must be equal in magnitude, hence \[3.2\left(\frac{R}{R+15\,\text{k}\Omega}\right)=2.2\] \[\frac{R}{R+15\,\text{k}\Omega}=\frac{22}{32}=\frac{11}{16}\] \[16R=11R+165\,\text{k}\Omega\] \[5R=165\,\text{k}\Omega\] \[\boxed{R=33\,\text{k}\Omega}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: A transistor having \(\alpha=0.99\) and \(V_{BE}=0.7\,\text{V}\), is used in the circuit of the figure. The value of the collector current (in mA) will be
questions.explanation: Given, \(\alpha=0.99\) and \(V_{BE}=0.7\,\text{V}\) Hence, \[\beta=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha} =\frac{0.99}{0.01} =99\] Assume that the transistor is operating in saturation. Thus taking \(V_{CE(\text{sat})}=0.2\,\text{V}\) Applying KVL in the loop containing the base-emitter junction, \[-12+1\,\text{k}(I_B+I_{C(\text{sat})})+10\,\text{k}I_B+0.7 +1\,\text{k}(I_B+I_{C(\text{sat})})=0\] \[12\,\text{k}I_B+2\,\text{k}I_{C(\text{sat})}=11.3 \tag{1}\] Applying KVL in the loop containing \(V_{CE(\text{sat})}\), \[-12+1\,\text{k}(I_B+I_{C(\text{sat})}) +1\,\text{k}I_{C(\text{sat})} +0.2 +1\,\text{k}(I_B+I_{C(\text{sat})})=0\] \[2\,\text{k}I_B+3\,\text{k}I_{C(\text{sat})}=11.8 \tag{2}\] Solving (1) and (2), \[I_B=0.321\,\text{mA}, \qquad I_{C(\text{sat})}=3.71\,\text{mA}\] The maximum collector current supported by the available base current is \[\beta I_B =99\times0.321 =31.779\,\text{mA}\] Since \(\beta I_B>I_{C(\text{sat})},\) the transistor is indeed in saturation. \[\boxed{I_C=3.71\,\text{mA}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: To obtain very high input and output impedances in a feedback amplifier, the mostly used feedback is
questions.explanation: In a current-series feedback amplifier, the output current is sampled and the feedback signal is applied in series at the input. Series mixing increases the input impedance, while current sampling increases the output impedance. Hence, both the input and output impedances are high. \[\boxed{(B)\;\text{Current-series}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: An RC-Coupled Amplifier is assumed to have a single-pole low frequency transfer function. The maximum lower-cutoff frequency allowed for the amplifier to pass \(50\,\text{Hz}\) square wave with no more than \(10\%\) tilt is Hz.
questions.explanation: Given, \(P=10\%,\) and \(f=50\,\text{Hz}\) The percentage tilt for a single-pole RC-coupled amplifier is, \[P=\frac{\pi f_L}{f}\times100\%\] Therefore, \[\frac{\pi f_L}{50}\times100\le10\] \[f_L\le\frac{10\times50}{\pi\times100}\] \[f_L\le1.59\,\text{Hz}\] Hence, the maximum allowable lower cut-off frequency is: \(1.59\) Hz \[\boxed{1.59\,\text{Hz}}\]

questions.ref: Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra Q1
questions.question: For the logic circuit shown in Figure, the output is equal to
questions.explanation:
Both left-side gates are XNOR gates. \[X_{1}=A \odot \overline{B} =\overline{A\oplus \overline{B}} =A\oplus B\] Similarly, \[X_{2}=A \odot \overline{B} =A\oplus B\] The final gate is also an XNOR gate, therefore \[Y=X_{1}\odot X_{2} =(A\oplus B)\odot(A\oplus B)=1\] \[\boxed{\text{(b) }1}\]
Key points
  • XNOR gate output is \(1\) when both inputs are identical.
  • \(A\odot\overline{B}=A\oplus B\).

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra Q2
questions.question: The minimum number of NAND gates required to implement the Boolean function \(A + A\overline{B} + A\overline{B}C,\) is equal to
questions.explanation: Taking \(A\) common from the given Boolean function: \[A + A\,\overline{B} + A\,\overline{B}\,C = A(1 + \overline{B} + \overline{B}\,C) = A(1) = A\] Since the expression simplifies directly to variable \(A\), no logic gates are required. Thus, the minimum number of NAND gates needed is zero. \[\boxed{\text{(A) zero}}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: A switch-tail ring counter is made by using a single D flip-flop. The resulting circuit is a
questions.explanation:
A switch-tail ring counter (also known as a Johnson counter) is formed by feeding the complemented output of the last flip-flop back into the input of the first flip-flop. When a single \(D\) flip-flop is used, its complemented output \(\overline{Q}\) is fed directly back into its own \(D\) input: \[D = \overline{Q}\] The characteristic equation of a \(D\) flip-flop is given by: \[Q_{next} = D\] Substituting \(D = \overline{Q}\) into the characteristic equation: \[Q_{next} = \overline{Q}\] This matches the behavior of a \(T\) flip-flop with its toggle input held high (\(T = 1\)), where the output toggles on every active clock edge: \[Q_{next} = T \oplus Q = 1 \oplus Q = \overline{Q}\] Thus, the resulting circuit behaves exactly as a \(T\) flip-flop. \[\boxed{\text{(D) T flip-flop}}\]
Key points
  • 1-Bit Johnson Counter: Formed by setting \(D = \overline{Q}\), which yields a modulus-2 counter (\(MOD\text{-}2\)).
  • Frequency Division: The output frequency is exactly half of the clock frequency (\(f_{out} = \frac{f_{clk}}{2}\)) with a \(50\%\) duty cycle.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question:
In each of the following questions, match each of the items, A, B and C with an appropriate item from 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. For an ADC, match the following
(A) Flash converter(1) requires a conversion time of the order of a few seconds
(B) Dual slope converter(2) requires a digital-to-analog converter
(C) Successive approximation converter(3) minimizes the effect of power supply interference
(4) requires a very complex hardware
(5) is a tracking A/D converter
questions.explanation:
Based on the key characteristics and hardware architectures of different Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs):
  • (A) Flash converter: Also known as a parallel comparator ADC, it operates at very high speeds but requires \(2^n - 1\) comparators for an \(n\)-bit resolution. This extensive parallel architecture makes it require a very complex hardware layout. \(\rightarrow\) (4) requires a very complex hardware
  • (B) Dual slope converter: As an integrating-type ADC, its continuous integration of the input voltage inherently rejects high-frequency periodic noise, thereby minimizing the effect of power supply interference. \(\rightarrow\) (3) minimizes the effect of power supply interference
  • (C) Successive approximation converter: This feedback-driven architecture utilizes an internal Successive Approximation Register (SAR) and a Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) to iteratively converge upon the correct binary representation. \(\rightarrow\) (2) requires a digital-to-analog converter
\[\boxed{\text{A-4, B-3, C-2}}\]
Key points
  • Flash ADC features the maximum speed but exhibits exponential hardware complexity (\(2^n - 1\) comparators).
  • Dual-Slope ADC offers high accuracy and noise immunity at the cost of slow conversion speed.
  • Successive Approximation Register (SAR) ADC incorporates a feedback loop containing a built-in DAC.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Families and Semiconductor Memories Q2
questions.question: The minimum number of MOS transistors required to make a dynamic RAM cell is
questions.explanation:
To determine the minimum number of MOS transistors required to design a Dynamic RAM (DRAM) cell:
  1. DRAM Cell Construction:
    A standard dynamic RAM (DRAM) cell stores a single bit of data as an electric charge on a storage capacitor (\(C_s\)). To read from or write to this capacitor, an access transistor is connected in series with it.
  2. The 1T1C Structure:
    The most widely used and basic DRAM configuration is the 1T1C (1-Transistor, 1-Capacitor) cell:
    • 1 MOS Transistor (Access Transistor): Acts as a switch controlled by the Word Line (WL) to connect the storage capacitor to the Bit Line (BL).
    • 1 Capacitor (Storage Capacitor): Stores the electric charge representing the binary state (\(0\) or \(1\)).
  3. Comparison with Static RAM (SRAM):
    Unlike SRAM, which requires a minimum of \(6\) transistors (6T) or \(4\) transistors (4T) with resistors to maintain bistable latch states, DRAM utilizes the simple 1T1C structure. This minimal transistor requirement makes DRAM significantly denser and cheaper per bit than SRAM.
Thus, the minimum number of MOS transistors required to make a dynamic RAM cell is \(1\). \[\boxed{\text{(A) 1}}\]
Key points
  • DRAM Cell: Formed by \(1\) MOS transistor and \(1\) capacitor (\(1\text{T}1\text{C}\)).
  • Refresh Cycle: Due to charge leakage in the capacitor over time, a DRAM cell must be refreshed periodically to preserve data.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: An 'Assembler' for a microprocessor is used for
options: assembly of processors in a production line
creation of new programs using different modules
translation of a program from assembly language to machine language
translation of a higher level language into English text
questions.explanation:
An Assembler is a software tool or program used in microprocessor systems to bridge the gap between low-level symbolic code and executable binary code.
  • It takes low-level assembly language programs (written using human-readable mnemonics like MOV, ADD, SUB) as the input source code.
  • It translates these instruction mnemonics into their corresponding binary operational codes (opcodes) and data patterns, converting it into machine language (object code) that the microprocessor can directly execute.
\[\boxed{\text{(C) translation of a programm from assembly language to machine language}}\]
Key points
  • Assembler: Converts Assembly Language \(\rightarrow\) Machine Language.
  • Compiler/Interpreter: Converts Higher-Level Language \(\rightarrow\) Machine/Intermediate Language.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: A 'DMA' transfer implies
options: direct transfer of data between memory and accumulator
direct transfer of data between memory and I/O devices without the use of \(\mu p\)
transfer of data exclusively within \(\mu P\) registers
A fast transfer of data between \(\mu P\) and I/O devices
questions.explanation:
Direct Memory Access (DMA) is a technique used in computer systems that allows high-speed input/output (I/O) devices to transfer data directly to or from the system memory.
  • Ordinarily, the microprocessor (\(\mu\text{P}\)) acts as an intermediary, fetching data from an I/O device into an internal register and then writing it to memory (or vice versa), which creates a significant bottleneck.
  • During a DMA transfer, the DMA controller requests control of the system buses via the HOLD signal. Once the microprocessor relinquishes control (HLDA), data is transferred directly between the memory and the I/O peripheral without involving or utilizing the microprocessor's internal processing circuitry.
Therefore, option (B) is the correct statement. \[\boxed{\text{(B) direct transfer of data between memory and I/O devices without the use of }\mu\text{p}}\]
Key points
  • DMA bypasses the CPU completely to maximize data transfer rates between fast peripheral devices and RAM.
  • Control signals like HOLD and HLDA in the 8085 microprocessor are dedicated exclusively to coordinating DMA operations.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: In a microprocessor, When a CPU is interrupted, it
options: acknowledges interrupt and branches of subroutine
acknowledges interrupt and waits for the next instruction from the interrupting device
questions.explanation:
When a microprocessor (such as the 8085) receives a hardware interrupt request via its INTR line, it goes through the following sequence:
  1. Complete Current Instruction: The CPU first finishes executing the instruction currently in progress.
  2. Interrupt Acknowledge: If interrupts are enabled, the CPU generates an interrupt acknowledge signal (\(\overline{\text{INTA}}\) goes low).
  3. Fetch Instruction from Device: During this acknowledge cycle, the CPU does not automatically know where to branch. Instead, it waits for the external interrupting device to place an instruction (typically a restart instruction like RST n or a CALL opcode) onto the data bus.
Once that external instruction is received from the device, the CPU executes it to push the program counter onto the stack and branch to the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR). Therefore, the immediate action upon acknowledgment is waiting for that instruction from the device. \[\boxed{\text{(D) acknowledges interrupt and waits for the next in-struction from the interrupting device}}\]
Key points
  • For the non-vectored interrupt (INTR), the branch address is not fixed internally; the CPU relies on the external device to provide the opcode during the \(\overline{\text{INTA}}\) cycle.
  • Option (B) would be true for internally vectored interrupts (like TRAP, RST 7.5), but option (D) perfectly generalizes the fundamental hardware handshake mechanism.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The transfer function of a linear system is the
options: Ratio of the output, \(V_0(t)\) and input \(V_i(t)\).
Ratio of the derivatives of the output and the input.
Ratio of the Laplace transform of the output and that of the input with all initial conditions zeroes.
questions.explanation: The transfer function is the ratio of the Laplace transform of the output to the Laplace transform of the input, under the strict assumption that all initial conditions are zero. \[\text{T.F.} = \frac{\mathcal{L}[\text{Output}]}{\mathcal{L}[\text{Input}]} \bigg|_{\text{initial conditions} = 0}\] \[\boxed{\text{(C) \ \ Ratio of the Laplace transform of the output and that of the input with all initial conditions zeroes}}\]

questions.question:
Common Data for Questions Q2.11.1 and Q6.11.1: The input-output transfer function of a plant \(H(s) = \dfrac{100}{s(s+10)^{2}}\). The plant is placed in a unity negative feedback configuration as shown in the figure below. The 2nd Question is given in Unit VI (Q6.11.1)

Signal flow graph is used to find
questions.explanation:
The signal flow graph (SFG) is a graphical representation of a set of linear algebraic equations. The main application of a signal flow graph is to determine the the transfer function. \[\boxed{\text{(C) \ transfer function of the system}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
Stability vs. Transfer Function: While the transfer function can be used to analyze stability (by looking at the poles), the SFG itself is a tool for finding the transfer function, not a direct method for determining stability.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The step error coefficient of a system \(G(s) = \dfrac{1}{(s + 6)(s + 1)}\) with unity feedback is
questions.explanation:
Method 1
The positional error constant \(K_{p}\) is defined as: \[K_{p} = \lim_{s \to 0} G(s)H(s)\] \[K_{p} = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{1}{(s + 6)(s + 1)}\] \[K_{p} = \frac{1}{(0 + 6)(0 + 1)} = \frac{1}{6}\]
Method 2
Shortcut Method: \[K_{p} = \frac{\text{Numerator constant}}{\text{Denominator constant}}\] Numerator constant \(= 1\); Denominator constant \(= 6\) \[K_{p} = \frac{1}{6}\]
\[\boxed{(A) \ \ \frac{1}{6}}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: For a second order system, damping ratio \((\xi)\), is \(0 < \xi < 1\), then the roots of the characteristic polynomial are
questions.explanation: The characteristic polynomial for a standard second order system is given by: \[s^2 + 2\xi\omega_{n}s + \omega_{n}^2 = 0\] When the damping ratio \((\xi)\) is in the range \(0 < \xi < 1\), the system is underdamped. The roots (poles) of the characteristic equation are complex conjugates: \[s_{1,2} = -\xi\omega_{n} \pm j\omega_{n}\sqrt{1 - \xi^2}\] Since the roots have both real and imaginary parts, they appear as a pair of complex conjugates in the \(s\)-plane.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: Non-minimum phase transfer function is defined as the transfer function
options: which has zeros in the right half \(s\)-plane.
which has zeros only in the left half \(s\)-plane.
which has poles in the right half \(s\)-plane.
which has poles in the left half \(s\)-plane.
questions.explanation: A non-minimum phase transfer function has at least one pole and/or one zero in the right half of the \(s\)-plane. Thus, both right half plane poles and right half plane zeros indicate non-minimum phase behaviour. Hence, both the given statements are technically correct. However, in objective type examinations, non-minimum phase systems are generally identified using right half plane zeros. \[\boxed{\text{(A) which has zeros in the right half }s\text{-plane.}}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: If the number of bits per sample in a PCM system is increased from \(n\) to \(n+1\), the improvement in signal-to-quantization noise ratio will be
questions.explanation:
Theory:
For a uniform PCM system, each additional bit halves the quantization step size, reducing quantization noise power by a factor of \(4\), which corresponds to an improvement of \(6\) dB in SQNR. For an \(n\)-bit PCM system, \[\left(\frac{S}{N_q}\right)_{\mathrm{dB}} = 1.8+6n\]For \((n+1)\) bits, \[\left(\frac{S}{N_q}\right)_{\mathrm{dB}} = 1.8+6(n+1)\]Hence, the improvement is \[\Delta\left(\frac{S}{N_q}\right)_{\mathrm{dB}} = \Big[1.8+6(n+1)\Big] - \Big[1.8+6n\Big]\]Therefore, \[\boxed{(B) 6~\mathrm{dB}}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: A PAM signal can be detected by using
questions.explanation:
Theory: PAM is recovered by extracting the average value of the sampled pulses using a low-pass filter or an integrator. A PAM signal consists of pulses whose amplitudes follow the message signal. [figure unavailable] An integrator performs averaging over each sampling interval and reconstructs the envelope of the sampled signal. [figure unavailable] Hence, an integrator (or equivalently a low-pass filter) is used to detect PAM signals. \[\boxed{\text{(B) an integrator}}\]
Key points
  • PAM information is carried in pulse amplitudes.
  • An integrator smooths the sampled waveform.
  • A low-pass filter performs the same reconstruction function.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use a band-pass or high-pass filter for PAM detection.
  • ADC is not the analog detector of PAM.
  • Remember that reconstruction requires averaging of pulse amplitudes.

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: A PLL can be used to demodulate
questions.explanation:
Theory: A PLL converts frequency variations of an FM signal into a proportional output voltage, thereby recovering the message signal. A Phase Locked Loop (PLL) consists of a phase detector, low-pass filter and voltage controlled oscillator (VCO). [figure unavailable] The phase detector generates an error voltage proportional to the instantaneous frequency difference between the incoming FM signal and the VCO output. After low-pass filtering, this error voltage is the recovered message signal. \[\boxed{\text{(C) FM signals}}\]
Key points
  • PLL is an FM demodulator.
  • Phase detector generates the error signal.
  • Low-pass filter extracts the message signal.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse PLL demodulation with coherent AM or DSB-SC detection.
  • PCM and PAM are not demodulated using a PLL.
  • Remember that the PLL tracks frequency variations, not amplitude variations.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: Copper behaves as a
options: conductor or dielectric depending on the applied electric field strength
conductor or dielectric depending on the frequency
conductor or dielectric depending on the electric current density
questions.explanation: A material is classified as a good conductor if the magnitude of the conduction current density is much larger than the displacement current density, which is equivalent to the condition: \[\frac{\sigma}{\omega\epsilon} \gg 1 \implies \sigma \gg \omega\epsilon\] For copper, the typical electrical parameters are: \[\sigma = 5.8 \times 10^{7}\,\text{S/m}\] \[\epsilon \approx \epsilon_{0} = 8.856 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F/m}\] Given these values, we can verify the condition \(\sigma \gg \omega\epsilon\) for a wide range of angular frequencies \(\omega\): \[\frac{\sigma}{\omega\epsilon} = \frac{5.8 \times 10^{7}}{\omega \times 8.856 \times 10^{-12}} \approx \frac{6.55 \times 10^{18}}{\omega}\] Even at very high (microwave) frequencies, for example at \(f = 100\,\text{GHz}\) (\(\omega \approx 6.28 \times 10^{11}\,\text{rad/s}\)), the ratio is still approximately \(10^{7}\), which is significantly greater than 1. Thus, copper behaves as a good conductor for all practical frequencies. \[\boxed{(A):\text{conductor always}}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The intrinsic impedance of a lossy dielectric medium is given by
questions.explanation:
The intrinsic impedance \(\eta\) of a medium is defined as the ratio of the phasor electric field intensity \(\vec{E}\) to the phasor magnetic field intensity \(\vec{H}\). For a general lossy dielectric medium, characterized by permeability \(\mu\), permittivity \(\epsilon\), and conductivity \(\sigma\), the intrinsic impedance is derived from Maxwell's equations as: \[\eta = \sqrt{\frac{j\omega\mu}{\sigma + j\omega\epsilon}}\] This expression accounts for both conduction current (\(\sigma\vec{E}\)) and displacement current (\(j\omega\epsilon\vec{E}\)). \[\boxed{(C)}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse \(\eta\) with the propagation constant \(\gamma = \sqrt{j\omega\mu(\sigma + j\omega\epsilon)}\).

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: An antenna, when radiating has a highly directional radiation pattern. When the antenna is receiving, its radiation pattern
questions.explanation: The concept described in the text is known as Antenna Reciprocity. This fundamental property of antennas states that the characteristics of an antenna, such as its radiation pattern, impedance, and directivity, are identical regardless of whether it is operating in the transmitting mode or the receiving mode. Essentially, if an antenna is designed to radiate energy in a specific direction with a certain pattern when fed a signal, it will, by the theorem of reciprocity, exhibit the exact same pattern when intercepting incoming electromagnetic waves from that same direction. \[\boxed{(C):\text{Is the same}}\]
